questions.stem: The nurse is planning assignments on a medical unit. Which task is most appropriate to delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel?

options.label: A
options.text: Obtaining vital signs on a client who is two days post-appendectomy and stable
options.rationale: Vital signs on a stable client are a routine, predictable task with a standard procedure, which is exactly what may be delegated to unlicensed assistive personnel.

options.label: B
options.text: Teaching a newly diagnosed client how to draw up and inject insulin
options.rationale: Teaching requires nursing judgment and evaluation of learning, so it must stay with the registered nurse and cannot be delegated.

options.label: C
options.text: Assessing a client's pain thirty minutes after an intravenous opioid dose
options.rationale: Assessment, especially reassessment after a high-alert medication, is a nursing responsibility that cannot be delegated to unlicensed staff.

questions.teachingPoint: Delegate stable, routine, predictable tasks; keep assessment, teaching, evaluation and nursing judgment with the registered nurse.

questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients at the start of the shift. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.label: A
options.text: A client with pneumonia whose oxygen saturation is 92 percent on 2 liters, unchanged from baseline
options.rationale: A saturation at the client's known baseline is stable and expected, so this client can safely wait a few minutes.

options.label: B
options.text: A client one day after abdominal surgery with new shortness of breath and chest pain
options.rationale: New shortness of breath with chest pain after surgery may signal a pulmonary embolism, an airway and circulation emergency that must be assessed first.

options.label: C
options.text: A client with diabetes whose fasting glucose is 180 milligrams per deciliter and who is asking for breakfast
options.rationale: A moderately elevated glucose needs attention but is not immediately life-threatening, so this client is a lower priority.

questions.teachingPoint: Use the ABCs and the principle of new versus expected findings: a new, unexpected change in airway, breathing or circulation always comes first.

questions.stem: A client scheduled for surgery says, 'I signed the consent form, but I still do not understand what the surgeon is going to do.' What is the nurse's best action?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain the details of the procedure and its risks to the client
options.rationale: Explaining the procedure, its risks and alternatives is the responsibility of the provider performing it, not the nurse witnessing the signature.

options.label: B
options.text: Reassure the client that the surgeon has performed this operation many times
options.rationale: Reassurance does not address the client's lack of understanding and would allow surgery to proceed without truly informed consent.

options.label: C
options.text: Notify the surgeon that the client needs more information before the procedure proceeds
options.rationale: Consent is valid only when it is informed; the nurse advocates for the client by contacting the surgeon so the client's questions are answered before surgery.

questions.teachingPoint: The nurse witnesses the signature and verifies understanding; when understanding is missing, the nurse stops the process and involves the provider.
